Welcome from the Chair

Studying the systems that hold the planet together — and the ones that are coming apart.

Coastal field sites, instrumented oceans, ice cores from two continents.

For nearly eighty years, EAMS faculty and students have worked across the boundary between rock, water, and air — from the granite cliffs at Cobbett Point to the Labrador Sea. Our department is small enough that every undergraduate has a research home by sophomore year, and large enough to host a thirty-foot piston core and a full atmospheric chemistry suite. Whether you are deciding on a major, considering graduate study, or visiting the building for a seminar, we are glad to have you.

— Prof. Asha Mahalingam
Chair · Henry C. Brennan Professor of Physical Oceanography

Research Spotlight

Listening to the overturning slowdown

After eight years of moored observations across the western boundary, the Mahalingam Lab is publishing the first continuous regional record of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.

Most published estimates of the AMOC's recent decline have leaned heavily on the RAPID array at 26°N. Prof. Mahalingam's group has, since 2017, kept seven bottom-mounted instruments at the western edge of the subpolar gyre, recording temperature, salinity, and bottom currents at fifteen-minute resolution. Their new Nature Geoscience paper combines those moorings with tracer chemistry from annual ship visits to reconstruct a regional overturning index back to 1820, finding a step-decline that begins decades earlier than the global average suggests.
